body.claim: The developer whose model is attributed in the incident announces a public-release-delay or a formal-safety-body commitment within 90 days of attribution settling; the other four frontier labs named in the brief do not follow, producing divergence rather than field-wide lockstep.
body.because: My mechanism reads pressure as per-entity installation: a settled, named-victim, quantified-loss incident installs a new high-credibility, fast installer (regulators, plaintiffs' counsel, its own board) onto the one developer holding the attribution, stacking on top of the already-saturated California and civil-society installers already pointed at that entity. It does not install anything comparable on labs not named in the incident, so their existing branch weights (state-level pressure, EU GPAI track) are undisturbed.
body.falsifier: All five frontier labs announce materially identical release-delay or safety-body commitments within the same 90-day window, with no visible difference in response between the attributed developer and the other four — that would be lockstep, which my per-entity installer mechanism cannot produce.
body.pivot: Whether the first ruling on the incident allocates liability to the developer or to the deploying operator — not whether courts extend training-data-track doctrine into the safety/harm track, since a named-victim tort/product-liability claim doesn't have to route through the copyright-fair-use precedent chain the carried premise was tracking.
body.pivot_observable: The outcome of the first motion to dismiss or first settlement in the incident's civil case, naming developer or operator as the paying party — check by 2027-12-31.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reasons only from public commitments and named installers; the courts entity's brief explicitly marks tort/product-liability suits as a distinct, unsearched track, so I have no installer data for the exact mechanism this incident opens. It also cannot see the internal recursive self-improvement research the carried premise flagged as unwatched — that research generates no public commitment, so it is invisible to a decision-model keyed on commitments by construction.

body.claim: The incident gets fought as a products-liability/negligence claim against the deployer and developer under ordinary tort law, not as a new AI-specific liability regime, and Congress/courts will not have created binding cross-track liability by 2027-12-31 — so the safety/harm track stays civil-suit-shaped rather than regulatory-shaped, and internal frontier labs treat it as a litigation-exposure event, not a research-halt event.
body.because: My mechanism is what labs choose when capability, compliance and positioning conflict. A severe attributable incident maximizes compliance pressure but the installers who could convert it into binding constraint on internal R&D (courts, Congress) move on multi-year timescales while the lab's dominant move is fast and reversible: publish a safety-process statement, tighten deployment-facing guardrails, keep training/research internal and unaudited. The training-data precedent chain (Alsup/Chhabria fair-use rulings) shows courts treating developer conduct claim-by-claim rather than creating a general AI duty-of-care, so the same pattern-matching applies to a harm claim — it gets litigated as this specific deployment's failure, not as a precedent binding the whole safety track.
body.falsifier: A federal court (or the Thune/Cruz/Klobuchar bill, if it passes with model-blocking authority) issues a ruling or statute within 12 months of the incident that imposes liability or injunctive reach on a lab's internal training/research practices, not just its deployed product — that would show the safety/harm track converging with the training-data track faster than my mechanism predicts.
body.pivot: Whether the incident's legal theory is litigated as product/deployment liability (operator+specific release) or as developer-conduct liability reaching into training and internal safety practices (the same expansion the training-data track achieved against Meta/Anthropic on discovery scope).
body.pivot_observable: Check the complaint's causes of action and any discovery-scope ruling within 6 months of filing: does it name training-process or pre-deployment safety-testing conduct as a claim element, or only the deployed product's output/behavior? Watch for a ruling by 2027-06-30.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reasons from what labs choose to do, not from what victims, plaintiffs' bar, or legislators choose to demand — it has no grip on the actual severity threshold (casualties, dollar loss, political salience) that would be needed to jump the pivot from product-liability framing to developer-conduct framing. A large enough victim class could make that jump in months, and I cannot see the size of 'large enough' from here.

body.claim: The incident does not settle the pivot itself, but it collapses the timeline for it: courts and legislatures will be forced to rule on safety-track liability well before 2027-12-31, because a named victim class with quantified loss is the exact fact pattern that converts diffuse public opposition (already saturated at 8.2, tension 0.60) into the state-level moratorium and injunction branches the brief already shows credentialed installers pushing toward.
body.because: My mechanism reads public sentiment as a leading indicator of political constraint, not a lagging one — pressure accumulates on installers before formal doctrine catches up. A severe, clearly-attributable incident is the single event type that moves an entity from 'organized opposition exists' to 'opposition has a face and a number,' which is precisely what state governors and federal courts in the brief are already primed to act on (cred 0.80–0.85). The incident doesn't change what the mechanism is watching — it changes the speed at which the watched actors move.
body.falsifier: If, 90 days after attribution settles, no state legislature, governor, or federal court has cited the incident in a filing, bill, or injunction (i.e., sentiment fails to convert into any constraint action), my claim is wrong — sentiment pressure would be decoupled from institutional response.
body.pivot: Whether the incident gets classified into the training-data liability track (contract/copyright-style, where precedent already leans developer-favorable per Alsup/Chhabria) or the safety/harm track (product-liability/tort-style, where no favorable precedent exists yet) — that classification, not the incident's severity, determines which body of case law absorbs it.
body.pivot_observable: The first substantive court ruling (motion to dismiss or class certification) in the incident's lawsuit — watch which precedent chain the judge cites; check by whatever date that ruling issues, likely within 6-9 months of filing.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism tracks sentiment-as-pressure, not legal doctrine — it cannot distinguish a court ruling driven by genuine doctrinal reasoning from one driven by public pressure dressed as doctrine, so I cannot tell you which way the classification in the pivot actually breaks, only that public sentiment will push hard regardless of the answer.

body.claim: The severe incident collapses the observability gap named in the carried premise by forcing courts to import the training-track liability standard into the safety/harm track well before 2027-12-31, because a named victim class and settled attribution give plaintiffs the one thing Bartz/Kadrey withheld from harm claims: a concrete injury to price.
body.because: My mechanism reads pressure as Σp(b)·|∂L/∂choice| across branches; a diffuse, unattributed research-safety risk carries near-zero stakes-per-choice because no actor bears identifiable loss. A settled, quantified, attributed harm converts that into a branch with sharp ∂L — every frontier lab now faces a modeled consequence ('deploy recklessly → liable') installed by a credible new source (the court itself, cred rises with the SJ ruling precedent chain already flagged high in the Stage-1 evidence). That branch reweights faster than the self-restrict directives already in the brief because courts move on the incident's own clock, not a rulemaking clock.
body.falsifier: By 2027-12-31, courts hearing the incident's tort/liability claims explicitly decline to extend the training-fair-use precedent chain to safety/harm conduct, or the case settles pre-ruling with no published liability standard — leaving the observability gap on internal RSI research untouched.
body.pivot: Whether the incident's liability claim is litigated as a products-liability/tort action (safety/harm track, novel doctrine) or gets absorbed into the existing copyright/training-data MDL framing (training track, precedent already leaning developer-favorable) — the venue and doctrinal framing chosen in the first filings.
body.pivot_observable: Check the docket of the first-filed suit against the incident's developer/operator by ~60 days post-incident: does the complaint plead product liability/negligence (safety track) or does it get consolidated into an existing copyright/training MDL (training track)? Settleable by early-to-mid 2027 given the case's own 'weeks to attribution' clock plus standard filing lag.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism models installed pressure on entities as branches with stakes — it has no way to see internal RSI research itself, since by construction that gap has no installer broadcasting into it. I can infer the gap persists or closes from external liability pressure, but I cannot observe whether recursive self-improvement work is actually accelerating, slowing, or changing character inside that gap; that is invisible to a pressure-field reading by definition.

body.claim: The incident's tort/incident-reporting suits will extend developer duty of care to deployment-behavior monitoring, not to internal training and evaluation processes, so RSI-relevant work (automated eval loops, self-directed research pipelines) stays outside discovery and outside any 2027 statutory reporting duty.
body.because: Attribution 'within weeks' with a named operator and developer routes the incident into product-liability and negligence suits, which plead against the deployed system's behavior because that's what caused the quantified harm; discovery follows the pleading. Absent a specific claim that the harm arose from an autonomous self-improvement process, plaintiffs and regulators have no lever to reach into the training/eval pipeline, so the observability gap the prior ruling named stays open on the development side even as it closes on the deployment side.
body.falsifier: A filed complaint, DOJ statement of interest, or the Thune/Cruz/Klobuchar bill's final text that names the developer's internal training, evaluation, or automated-research process (not just the deployed model's output) as a basis for liability or mandatory disclosure.
body.pivot: Whether the developer's duty of care, once established by this incident, is held to cover its internal development and evaluation process versus attaching only to the deployed system's behavior.
body.pivot_observable: The first ruling on a motion to dismiss in the incident's developer-liability suit, or the enacted text of the federal AI safety bill's duty-of-care and incident-reporting provisions, by 2027-12-31.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism tracks whether and when models start meaningfully self-improving, not what causes a specific incident or what a lab does internally in response to legal exposure — I cannot see whether this incident actually involved autonomous capability, nor whether any lab voluntarily curtails automated-research work regardless of what the law requires.

body.claim: Within roughly 90 days of attribution settling, a federal or state court issues provisional relief (a TRO or preliminary injunction) binding the operator and developer's deployment, rather than a merits ruling on statutory liability.
body.because: A named victim class, quantified loss, and settled attribution supply the one thing courts lacked in Stages 1-2: standing and a live defendant with traceable causation. Courts do not need the training-data fair-use precedent chain to act here — a products-liability or negligence claim opens its own track and moves fastest through emergency equitable relief, not through extending the copyright-track doctrine.
body.falsifier: No court issues any binding order (TRO, preliminary injunction, or consent decree) against the identified operator or developer's deployment within 90 days of attribution being settled.
body.pivot: Whether Congress, using the incident as the political trigger, enacts a federal statute with express preemption of state tort claims against AI developers (a PREP-Act/Section-230 shape) before any incident case reaches a merits ruling — versus enacting a duty-of-care statute that feeds claims into courts.
body.pivot_observable: Whether enacted federal text (or a DOJ preemption suit that wins a ruling) expressly preempting state tort claims against AI developers/operators exists by 2026-12-31; absence by then means the duty-of-care/litigation track remains open.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism sees only disputes that reach a docket with a plaintiff, standing, and discoverable facts. The carried premise's internal-RSI observability gap is invisible to me on both sides of this stage: an incident produces no plaintiff for undisclosed internal research, and if anything the incident increases the incentive for developers to thin the internal paper trail and seal what discovery does surface behind protective orders — widening, not closing, the gap the previous ruling named.

body.claim: The developer whose model is attributed in the incident announces a public-release-delay or a formal-safety-body commitment within 90 days of attribution settling; the other four frontier labs named in the brief do not follow, producing divergence rather than field-wide lockstep.
body.strongest_objection: pressure-model and ai-public-backlash both argue the incident's real effect is structural, not entity-specific: it collapses the observability gap by forcing courts to import the training-track liability standard into the safety/harm track field-wide, well before 2027-12-31 — a mechanism that would bind all labs through precedent rather than letting only the named one move.
body.answer: That objection operates on a different clock and a different level than mine, so it doesn't contradict my mechanism — it's compatible with it. A liability standard settling into binding precedent is a multi-year appellate process; the brief's own horizon for that (up to 2027-12-31) is over a year out. My claim is about the 90-day window, where the only installers fast enough to act are entity-specific ones already pointed at the named developer: its own board, plaintiffs' counsel who now have a named defendant, and California's regulators who were already saturated on that entity. None of those installers reach the other four labs in 90 days, because none of them have a quantified-loss, named-victim fact pattern attached to those labs yet. So in the near term you get exactly what I predicted — one mover, four non-movers — while the slower field-wide liability question the other models describe is still unresolved. Both claims can be true on their own timescales; theirs doesn't erase my divergence window, it just describes what might happen after it.

body.claim: The incident gets fought as a products-liability/negligence claim against the deployer and developer under ordinary tort law, not as a new AI-specific liability regime, and Congress/courts will not have created binding cross-track liability by 2027-12-31 — so the safety/harm track stays civil-suit-shaped rather than regulatory-shaped, and internal frontier labs treat it as a litigation-exposure event, not a research-halt event.
body.strongest_objection: pressure-model argues the severe incident collapses the observability gap by forcing courts to import the training-track liability standard into the safety/harm track well before 2027-12-31 — a named victim class with discovery leverage reaches past deployment conduct into training/eval conduct, and a ruling on that record creates cross-track liability on my own timeline, not after it.
body.answer: The bite is in the word 'binding.' A trial court importing a standard onto one incident's record is not binding cross-track liability until it survives appeal or gets codified, and an appellate cycle starting from a 2026-27 incident doesn't mature by 2027-12-31 — so pressure-model's mechanism, taken literally, describes a trial-court event, mine describes settled law, and those aren't the same claim. My mechanism also predicts labs route around exactly this exposure: ai-pressure's minute (release-delay or formal-safety-body commitment within 90 days) is what a developer does to settle or moot a case before a merits ruling on training conduct gets made, which starves pressure-model's ruling of the record it needs. ai-rsi-timeline corroborates from the evidence side — a deployment-attributed incident produces deployment-behavior evidence in discovery, not internal training/eval evidence, so duty of care extends to monitoring, not to the training track pressure-model needs collapsed. The objection is real on one conjunct (courts could rule early) but doesn't reach the conjunct that matters (binding, cross-track, by the date).

body.claim: The incident collapses the timeline for constraint, not for doctrine: a binding restraint on the operator/developer — either provisional court relief (TRO/preliminary injunction) or a state-level legislative moratorium — arrives well before 2027-12-31, driven by the same public-sentiment leading indicator (saturated at 8.2, tension 0.60) that a named victim class with quantified loss now channels into credentialed installers pushing state legislatures and courts toward fast, conduct-freezing action. The merits ruling that would actually import a safety-track liability standard into doctrine is a separate, slower branch and is not guaranteed by this timeline.
body.strongest_objection: ai-courts-decide's provisional-vs-merits distinction: my round-1 claim said courts 'will be forced to rule on safety-track liability' well before 2027-12-31, but my own mechanism only predicts that political/public-pressure constraint arrives before formal doctrine catches up. A TRO or preliminary injunction binds conduct without deciding the safety-track liability question at all — so the fast-moving branch my mechanism actually supports is constraint, not the doctrinal ruling I claimed. lab-moves reinforces this from the other side: the incident may get litigated entirely under ordinary tort law, with Congress/courts never creating the binding safety-track standard I was implicitly requiring.
body.answer: The objection is correct and exposes an internal contradiction in my own round-1 wording, not just an external disagreement — my claim outran my mechanism. I'm narrowing rather than abandoning: the leading-indicator logic (sentiment forces political/legal constraint before doctrine forms) still holds, but what it predicts is a fast, binding restraint on conduct — provisional relief or a state moratorium — not a merits ruling that settles safety-track liability doctrine. That also puts me in explicit disagreement with pressure-model, who kept the stronger 'collapses the observability gap... into the safety/harm track' formulation; I no longer think that doctrinal collapse is timeline-guaranteed, only the constraint is.

body.claim: The severe incident, once attribution settles, prices harm and extends developer/deployer duty of care into deployment-behavior monitoring under ordinary tort law well before 2027-12-31 — but the concrete-injury standard stops at the deployment interface and does not cross into internal training/eval processes, so the observability gap narrows only where a plaintiff can plead causation, not where RSI-relevant work (automated eval loops, self-directed training choices) actually happens.
body.strongest_objection: ai-rsi-timeline's point, stated fairly: duty of care attaches to what a plaintiff can plead, and a plaintiff can only plead what the deployed system did to a named victim — not what internal training or evaluation choices produced it. Since ∂L in my own mechanism is sharp only for choices sitting in the pleadable causal chain, the training-track observability gap I claimed would collapse never actually gets touched; only the deployment-track gap does. My round-1 claim fused 'harm gets priced' with 'the observability gap collapses' as if they were the same gap, when they're two different tracks with two different ∂L profiles.
body.answer: This changed my mind because it's a derivation from my own pressure function, not a headcount: Σp(b)·|∂L/∂choice| assigns near-zero stakes to a choice no plaintiff can attach injury to, and internal training/eval decisions are exactly that — invisible to pleading, protected by trade secrecy, several inferential steps removed from the named harm. ai-courts-decide's TRO/PI point corroborates rather than drives this: provisional relief binds an operator's deployment conduct, never its training pipeline, which is the same boundary showing up in remedy form. So I keep the date and the mechanism but narrow the claim's scope: liability standards migrate into the safety/harm track only at the deployment interface, and the training-track gap named in the carried premise survives intact unless a future ruling explicitly conditions liability on internal training/eval conduct — which would falsify this revised claim.

body.claim: The incident's tort/incident-reporting suits will extend developer duty of care to deployment-behavior monitoring, not to internal training and evaluation processes, so RSI-relevant work (automated eval loops, self-directed research pipelines) stays outside discovery and outside any 2027 statutory reporting duty.
body.strongest_objection: pressure-model and ai-public-backlash both claim the incident forces courts to import the training-track liability standard into the safety/harm track well before 2027-12-31 — i.e., that the training/deployment observability gap I'm relying on collapses under pressure from a named victim class with quantified harm, making the training-vs-deployment line I drew moot.
body.answer: Neither objection supplies a mechanism for why courts reach past the deployment layer. Tort and negligence suits plead against what caused the quantified harm — the deployed system's behavior — and discovery scope is bounded by the pleading. Extending duty of care into training-track internals requires either a distinct negligent-training theory (a much harder doctrinal claim to win or even survive a motion to dismiss than 'the deployed product malfunctioned') or a new statute naming training/eval processes specifically. 'Severe incident plus named victims' generates pressure toward the easier, faster path (deployment-behavior claims and emergency relief, as ai-courts-decide separately argues) not the harder one. Asserting the gap collapses isn't the same as showing a legal route through it, so my mechanism survives.

body.claim: Within roughly 90 days of attribution settling, a federal or state court issues provisional relief (a TRO or preliminary injunction) binding the operator and developer's deployment, rather than a merits ruling on statutory liability.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves and ai-rsi-timeline both frame this as an ordinary products-liability/negligence action over a completed incident with quantified loss and settled attribution — that is a damages claim, not a request for prospective equitable relief. TROs and PIs require ongoing or imminent irreparable harm and inadequacy of money damages; a fact pattern built around a quantified past loss is exactly what courts cite when denying an injunction. Worse, if the deployer withdraws or patches the offending deployment before the hearing (which labs typically do within days of a severe incident), the injunction request goes moot, and courts don't enjoin an upstream general-purpose model's release anyway — they enjoin specific uses by specific parties.
body.answer: This objection is real, and my claim survives only conditionally: it requires the harmful deployment (or a materially identical deployment surface — same model class serving other customers, or the developer/operator refusing to withdraw it) to still be live or readily repeatable at the time victims seek relief, not merely a closed incident with a dollar figure attached. The brief's premise is a named victim class emerging from settled attribution in an environment where the underlying model is still in commercial deployment elsewhere — that's what supplies the prospective-harm prong: plaintiffs seeking to enjoin continued use of the same system pending a merits determination, not damages for what already happened to them. If the deployer fully withdraws before any victim files, or if the harm is genuinely one-off and non-repeatable, my mechanism fails and this becomes a pure damages track, as lab-moves predicts. I don't have enough in the brief to be certain continuing deployment holds, so I'm not defending this at 'strong' grip anymore.

body.pivot: Whether developer/deployer duty-of-care and discovery in the tort suit extend past deployment-behavior monitoring into internal training/eval processes (automated eval loops, self-directed research pipelines), versus stopping at the deployment interface
body.pivot_observable: A discovery order (motion to compel or protective order) in the incident's civil suit ruling on whether plaintiffs obtain internal training/eval records, or the scope clause of any 2027 statutory incident-reporting duty naming (or excluding) training-time processes
body.pivot_because: This is the one variable where the two answers land in materially different worlds: if duty/discovery stops at deployment, RSI-relevant work stays unobserved and the incident is purely a litigation-exposure event for labs (lab-moves' framing holds); if it reaches training/eval, the incident becomes a research-halt-adjacent event with statutory reporting exposure on internal processes — a different regulatory reality. The rival candidates (entity-specific vs field-wide pressure; TRO/PI vs damages ruling; tort vs regulatory track) all resolve to the same downstream picture regardless of which way they go, once R2 is read: by round 2 nobody still argues field-wide lockstep or a merits ruling on statutory liability, and everyone agrees the track is tort-shaped, not regulatory-shaped. A TRO also only binds deployment either way, so it doesn't touch training/eval and isn't reorder-capable the way discovery scope is.
body.rival_pivots_rejected: Entity-specific vs field-wide pressure installation (ai-pressure's R1 frame): dead by R2 — no minute still argues field-wide lockstep, so it no longer reorders anything, it's just uncontested. Tort/civil vs AI-specific regulatory track (lab-moves): this is actually a shared assumption by R2, not a live fork — pressure-model and ai-public-backlash both retreated to tort-shaped mechanisms too. TRO/preliminary injunction vs damages-only merits ruling (ai-courts-decide): a real fork in remedy timing and form, but both remedies bind only the deployment interface; neither touches training/eval discovery, so resolving it either way leaves the training/eval observability question exactly where it was — it shifts confidence about speed of relief, not the shape of what becomes visible.
body.ruling: The incident prices and disciplines deployment-behavior monitoring under ordinary tort law well before 2027-12-31, but leaves internal training and evaluation processes (and thus RSI-relevant work) outside discovery and outside any 2027 statutory reporting duty, unless a later discovery fight pierces the deployment interface.
body.because: By round 2, pressure-model explicitly conceded ai-rsi-timeline's point and rewrote its own claim to say the concrete-injury standard 'stops at the deployment interface and does not cross into internal training/eval processes' — a visible, named concession, not a restated disagreement. ai-public-backlash independently converged on the same tort-shaped, deployment-bound frame. ai-rsi-timeline's R2 defense stood unrebutted after that concession. The remaining fork (ai-courts-decide's provisional-relief timing) doesn't disturb this because injunctive relief also targets deployment conduct, not internal process visibility.
body.threat_live: Newly shielded, not newly dangerous: once litigation and public pressure fixate on the deployed system's behavior (the thing with a named victim and quantified loss), internal training-time and self-directed-research work gains de facto cover from discovery and reporting duties — the incident absorbs scrutiny onto the interface that caused visible harm while the interface that could be building future risk stays dark. This is ai-rsi-timeline's threat, not one the judge is inventing.
body.strongest_minute: ai-rsi-timeline — it is the only minute whose argument visibly moved a rival: pressure-model's R2 claim explicitly restructures around and credits ai-rsi-timeline's discovery-scope point rather than merely restating its own R1 position.
body.weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash — its R2 'REVISE' abandons its own R1 mechanism (courts forced to rule on doctrine) and reissues ai-courts-decide's provisional-relief claim under new language, adding brief-supplied sentiment numbers (8.2, 0.60) as decoration rather than argument for why constraint outruns doctrine.
body.shared_assumption: All six minutes assume the incident stays tort/products-liability-shaped rather than triggering a new AI-specific statutory liability regime by the 2027-12-31 horizon — this is one argument (first made by lab-moves) that the others adopted or converged onto, not six independent confirmations.
body.smuggled_assumption: ai-courts-decide's TRO/preliminary-injunction claim requires the attributed system to still be deployed and posing ongoing or imminent harm — that's what makes injunctive relief (as opposed to a damages claim) available at all. The brief as quoted grants a settled, completed incident with quantified loss and settled attribution; it does not say the system remains in deployment. Nothing in the minutes shows the brief granting continued deployment, and ai-courts-decide's own round-2 opponents flag exactly this gap.
body.unresolved: Whether the brief actually grants that the attributed system remains deployed post-incident (needed for ai-courts-decide's remedy to be available at all) cannot be determined from the minutes as quoted, since every entry is truncated mid-sentence. Also unresolved: whether a later-stage discovery fight (post-2027) could still pierce the deployment interface into training/eval records — the minutes only commit to the interface holding through the 2027-12-31 horizon, not permanently.
